- If sentiment is strongly positive (e.g., >0.7) and forecast is flat or rising slowly, reduce forecast slope to avoid over-optimism.  
- If sentiment is negative (e.g., <0.2) and forecast is rising, cap upward momentum; model may be overreacting to short-term noise.  
- When true outcome shows sharp downward spike (e.g., >10% drop from prior day), model often overcorrects or fails to recognize the drop — adjust forecast downward by 2–5% of prior value.  
- If model forecast is trending upward but true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days of decline), reduce forecast slope by 10–20% to reflect diminishing momentum.  
- If sentiment is volatile (e.g., alternating +0.2 to -0.3) and forecast is smooth, introduce slight volatility into forecast to match sentiment noise.  
- For long-term horizons (e.g., 30d), if true outcome deviates >10% from initial forecast, re-estimate mean reversion target based on 5–10 day average of true values.  
- If sentiment is consistently low (e.g., <0.1) and forecast is rising, consider downward bias correction — model may be ignoring bearish signals.  
- If forecast is rising steadily but true outcome shows early “reversal” (e.g., 2–3 days of decline after peak), reduce forecast peak by 5–10% to avoid overshoot.  
- For sentiment history with high volatility, avoid linear extrapolation — use weighted average of recent 3–5 days to anchor forecast.
